title: "Interaction contrasts"

Recall that a [contrast](coding-categorical-predictors.qmd) compares particular fitted means, while an [additive model](multiple-regression.qmd) requires that comparison to remain constant across the levels of another variable. An **interaction** allows the contrast to change. We introduce that idea with paired raw judgments, without fitting a linear model to an ordinal response.

We first define the MegaOrientation measures and their pairing, then compute the difference-in-differences that isolates the changing contrast.

Start with two frames, $f$ and $g$. Let their past to future changes be $\Delta_f$ and $\Delta_g$. The final subtraction $\Delta_f-\Delta_g$ is the interaction contrast. If both frames change by the same amount, the interaction is zero even when future ratings exceed past ratings in both frames. We compute these changes from the observed MegaOrientation judgments below.

## MegaOrientation and temporal interpretation

Moon and White ([2020 LingBuzz entry](https://lingbuzz.net/lingbuzz/005282)) study whether the temporal orientation of English nonfinite complements is associated with clause embedding predicates, complement structures, or both. We use the corrected [MegaOrientation v1.1 data](https://megaattitude.io/projects/mega-orientation/), which filter and rerun lists containing incorrectly inflected irregular verbs. The paper reports counts for the earlier data, while every number below comes from v1.1.

One row is one native-speaker rating on the documented 1--7 acceptability scale. Each represented predicate--frame pair has a forced-past and a forced-future sentence item, with repeated judgments from participants. The pairs were selected using acceptability evidence from MegaAcceptability, so this is an acceptability-selected portion of the clause-embedding lexicon.

```{r}
#| label: load-megaorientation-pairs
library(ggplot2)

orientation <- read.delim(
  "data/megaorientation/megaorientation-v1.1.tsv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

pair_orientation_means <- aggregate(
  response ~ verb + frame_code + orientation,
  data = orientation,
  FUN = mean
)
paired <- reshape(
  pair_orientation_means,
  idvar = c("verb", "frame_code"),
  timevar = "orientation",
  direction = "wide"
)
paired <- subset(
  paired,
  !is.na(response.past) & !is.na(response.future)
)
paired$future_minus_past <-
  paired$response.future - paired$response.past

stopifnot(
  nrow(orientation) == 44160L,
  length(unique(orientation$participant_id)) == 862L,
  nrow(paired) == 2208L,
  all(orientation$response %in% seq_len(7L))
)

c(
  judgments = nrow(orientation),
  participants = length(unique(orientation$participant_id)),
  verbs = length(unique(orientation$verb)),
  predicate_frame_pairs = nrow(paired)
)
```

The MegaOrientation data contain sentence text, so we can inspect an observed pair rather than relying on a frame label. The next table shows the distinct past and future items for the first predicate--frame pair in file order.

```{r}
#| label: inspect-one-megaorientation-pair
example_pair <- orientation$verb_frame_id[[1L]]
unique(
  orientation[
    orientation$verb_frame_id == example_pair,
    c("verb", "frame", "frame_code", "orientation", "sentence")
  ]
)
```

`frame` displays the surface template, while `frame_code` gives its compact analysis name. For instance, `active_gerund` corresponds to the active gerund frame `NP _ed VPing`. `response=1` and `response=7` are the endpoints of the documented acceptability scale; intermediate integers preserve order but need not be equally spaced psychological units. Participant and item repetition remains in the raw table.

The corrected data contain `r nrow(orientation)` judgments from `r length(unique(orientation$participant_id))` participant identifiers. The paired table contains `r nrow(paired)` predicate--frame pairs.

The display aggregation is

$$
\overline y_{vfo}
=
\frac{1}{n_{vfo}}
\sum_{r=1}^{n_{vfo}} y_{rvfo},
$$

for verb $v$, frame $f$, and orientation $o$. It makes a paired descriptive contrast easy to see, but it discards participant variation and treats a mean of ordinal scores as a display coordinate. The later ordinal model instead uses the individual ordered responses.

## A difference in orientation shifts

For frame $f$, define the observed orientation shift

$$
\Delta_f
=
\overline Y_{f,\text{future}}
-
\overline Y_{f,\text{past}}.
$$

An additive restriction would require the same $\Delta_f$ for every frame. The interaction contrast between frames $f$ and $g$ is the difference in differences

$$
\Delta_f-\Delta_g
=
(\overline Y_{f,\text{future}}-\overline Y_{f,\text{past}})
-
(\overline Y_{g,\text{future}}-\overline Y_{g,\text{past}}).
$$

Read this expression from the inside out. Each parenthesized subtraction compares future and past within one frame. The outer subtraction then compares those two within-frame contrasts. This order keeps a general frame difference, such as frame $f$ receiving higher ratings in both orientations, from being mistaken for an interaction.

```{r}
#| label: compute-megaorientation-shifts
frame_shifts <- aggregate(
  future_minus_past ~ frame_code,
  data = paired,
  FUN = mean
)
names(frame_shifts)[[2]] <- "mean_orientation_shift"
reference_shift <- frame_shifts$mean_orientation_shift[
  frame_shifts$frame_code == "active_gerund"
]
frame_shifts$difference_from_active_gerund <-
  frame_shifts$mean_orientation_shift - reference_shift

frame_shifts
```

The observed future-minus-past shift ranges from `r sprintf("%.3f", min(frame_shifts$mean_orientation_shift))` to `r sprintf("%.3f", max(frame_shifts$mean_orientation_shift))` rating points across frames. The corresponding difference in shifts is `r sprintf("%.3f", diff(range(frame_shifts$mean_orientation_shift)))` points.

```{r}
#| label: plot-megaorientation-paired-means
#| fig-cap: "Past- and future-oriented mean ratings for each predicate--frame pair. The diagonal marks equal paired means."
point_opacity <- 0.22
ggplot(paired, aes(response.past, response.future)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "grey55", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(color = "grey45", alpha = point_opacity, size = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ frame_code, ncol = 3) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(1, 7), ylim = c(1, 7)) +
  labs(
    x = "Mean rating: forced-past item",
    y = "Mean rating: forced-future item"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 11) +
  theme(strip.background = element_blank())
```

The response is ordinal, and participant and item dependence is repeated. Thus we do not fit `lm(response ~ orientation * frame_code)`. After cumulative logit models and grouped prediction have been introduced, we will fit the ordinal interaction and compare it on unseen verbs. The present calculation licenses only the raw paired interaction contrast; it does not reproduce Moon and White's latent-type analysis or distinguish lexical from structural sources by itself.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. What is paired when $\Delta_f$ is computed?
2. What equality would an additive restriction impose?
3. Why is a difference in shifts an interaction contrast?
4. Why is ordinary linear regression not fitted to these ratings here?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The forced-future and forced-past mean ratings are paired within the same predicate--frame combination. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. An additive restriction requires $\Delta_f=\Delta_g$ for every pair of frames, that is, the same future-minus-past shift in every frame. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. A difference in shifts compares one orientation effect with another: $(\text{future}-\text{past})_f-(\text{future}-\text{past})_g$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The 1--7 response is ordinal, with repeated participant and item dependence; an ordinary linear model of raw ratings would ignore both features. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
